procedural_history.originating_court: The case originated as a Writ Petition (Criminal) No. 191 of 2017 directly in the Supreme Court of India.
procedural_history.impugned_order: There was no lower court order challenged in this case, as it originated in the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: There were no High Court proceedings, as the case originated in the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court heard arguments from the petitioner (Manohar Lal Sharma, appearing in person), the respondents (Sanjay Leela Bhansali & Ors., represented by counsel), and took assistance from the Additional Solicitor General for the Union of India. The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the writ petition with no order as to costs, noting that the petition appeared to sensationalize the matter and was motivated by a desire for publicity.

directions: with no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Court should entertain a writ petition and pass an order of injunction directing the CBFC to delete a clip and prevent a movie's release after the CBFC has already granted a certificate.

facts: The Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC), the designated statutory authority, had already granted a certificate for the movie in question.
The petitioner filed a writ petition asking the Court to order the CBFC to delete a clip and to prevent the movie's release.
The content the petitioner objected to was something that had already been shown in the media and was being reflected in the film.
law: The right to freedom of speech and expression is sacrosanct and should not be ordinarily interfered with.
application: The Court reasoned that since the CBFC, as the proper statutory body, had already reviewed the film and granted a certificate, the Court should restrain itself from interfering with that decision.
Interfering with the release of a certified film would be an infringement on the sacrosanct right to freedom of speech and expression.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petition, holding that it should not entertain such a request or grant an injunction after the CBFC has already certified a film. The Court based its decision on the principle that freedom of speech is a sacrosanct right and that the judiciary should exercise restraint and not interfere with the functioning of the statutory body (CBFC) that has already performed its duty.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Court should entertain a writ petition and pass an order of injunction directing the CBFC to delete a clip and prevent a movie's release after the CBFC has already granted a certificate.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner filed a writ petition seeking an injunction to direct the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) to delete a clip and prevent the release of a movie.
respondent_arguments: The court's interference in the writ petition after the CBFC has already certified the film would be inappropriate and would amount to pre-judging the matter.

cases.case_name: Sudhir Kumar Saha v. Commissioner of Police and another
cases.principle: When a writ petition mentions dates of events, they constitute part of the pleadings.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a matter is pending for consideration before a statutory authority, it is a violation of the rule of law for people in power or public offices to comment on the issue, as this can create prejudice in the mind of the authority which is expected to make decisions with utmost objectivity.
obiter: No right is absolute, and any fetters for enjoying rights, particularly the right to freedom of speech, expression, and liberty, must be absolutely reasonable.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court's interference in the writ petition before the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC), the designated statutory authority, has made its decision would be improper, as it would tantamount to pre-judging the matter.
legal_tests_applied: It is settled in law that no right is absolute but the fetters for enjoying the rights should be absolutely reasonable more so when it relates to the right to freedom of speech and expression and right to liberty.
why_appellant_lost: The petition was filed prematurely, before the CBFC, the statutory authority, had taken a decision on the film's certification.
The Court's intervention would amount to pre-judging the matter, which it is not inclined to do.
The petition was deemed an abuse of the Public Interest Litigation process, motivated by a "hunger for publicity or some other hidden motive."
The pleadings in the petition were found to be "absolutely scwTilous, vexatious and untenable in law" and were struck from the record.
why_respondent_won: The Court accepted the respondent's position that judicial interference is inappropriate while the matter is pending consideration before the CBFC.
The CBFC is the proper statutory authority expected to make decisions with utmost objectivity as per the law, and the Court will not usurp its function.
The Court affirmed the principle that freedom of speech and expression is sacrosanct and should not be ordinarily interfered with through a pre-emptive injunction.
policy_considerations: Filing writ petitions before the statutory authority (CBFC) has made a decision is an abuse of public interest litigation that sullies the temple of justice and creates dents in the justice dispensation system.

Under the rule of law, when a matter is pending before a statutory authority for certification, responsible people in power or public offices should not comment on the issue, as it creates a sense of prejudice and is a violation of the rule of law.
